title: Leg 54 — Teton Valley to Yellowstone Gateway
subtitle: Blackfoot, Idaho Falls, Teton Valley, Grand Teton, Ashton, Island Park and West Yellowstone
preflightBriefing: Welcome aboard. Today we're leaving Pocatello and following the eastern Snake River Plain through Blackfoot and Idaho Falls before turning east toward Teton Valley. The Grand Teton range should become an unmistakable landmark well before Driggs, then we'll turn north with the mountains off the right side before crossing toward Ashton and Island Park. The final stretch carries us across an older Yellowstone volcanic center and into West Yellowstone. I'll stay quiet while you taxi and depart. Once you're airborne and settled, say Trip continue.

blocks.title: Leaving Pocatello
blocks.text: Pocatello is falling behind as we head northeast onto the eastern Snake River Plain. The broad floor ahead looks gentle compared with yesterday's mountain country, but it is the surface expression of millions of years of volcanism, faulting and sediment laid down between ranges.

blocks.title: Fort Hall country
blocks.text: This first stretch crosses the broader Fort Hall country, homeland of the Shoshone-Bannock peoples and a travel corridor long before highways or railroads. The open plain made movement easier than the mountain country around it, which is one reason routes kept converging here.

blocks.title: Basalt beneath the farms
blocks.text: Much of the plain beneath us is built from repeated basalt lava flows. Soil, windblown sediment and irrigated farmland now soften the surface, but the volcanic foundation is still there, fractured enough to store and move enormous quantities of groundwater.

blocks.title: Blackfoot ahead
blocks.text: Blackfoot is still about four miles ahead, almost directly along our path. It sits in one of the most productive agricultural parts of eastern Idaho, where irrigation turned the volcanic plain into country famous for potatoes, grain and other crops.

blocks.title: Blackfoot and Idaho potatoes
blocks.text: We're coming over Blackfoot now. The town even has an Idaho Potato Museum, housed in a 1913 Oregon Short Line railroad depot. The building is a neat little symbol of how railroads and agriculture grew together here: trains once moved both passengers and enormous amounts of farm freight through the valley.

blocks.title: Why the fields can exist here
blocks.text: The green geometry below depends on water as much as soil. Snowmelt from the surrounding mountains feeds rivers and irrigation systems, while the fractured basalt beneath the plain holds one of the region's great aquifers. The landscape looks agricultural, but its plumbing is deeply volcanic.

blocks.title: Idaho Falls ahead
blocks.text: Idaho Falls is still roughly six miles ahead. It is the largest city in eastern Idaho and sits directly on the Snake River, so the city should become a much more obvious visual anchor than the smaller farming communities behind us.

blocks.title: Idaho Falls and the Snake River
blocks.text: Idaho Falls should be close below now, spread along the Snake River. The modern city is the regional center for a huge surrounding area, but from the air the river is still the simplest way to read the city: development follows both banks while the broad agricultural plain continues beyond.

blocks.title: A city tied to nuclear research
blocks.text: Idaho Falls also became closely tied to the nuclear research complex west of town. The city today hosts the headquarters of Idaho National Laboratory, connecting this agricultural valley with the atomic-energy history we encountered near Arco on the previous leg.

blocks.title: North toward the Rexburg area
blocks.text: North of Idaho Falls, the plain narrows slightly and the terrain ahead starts pointing toward the Teton country. We are not over Rexburg itself; the city sits several miles north of our turning point, so this is better thought of as the southern edge of the Rexburg area.

blocks.title: Rexburg off the left
blocks.text: Rexburg is still off the left side, several miles north of our path. It was settled in 1883 and became an education center after a church academy opened in 1888. That school eventually evolved into today's Brigham Young University-Idaho.

blocks.title: The flood that changed Rexburg
blocks.text: Rexburg's modern history is inseparable from the Teton Dam disaster. In 1976 the dam northeast of town failed during its first filling, releasing a catastrophic flood that struck Rexburg, Sugar City and other communities. Eleven people died, and the failure became a major catalyst for the Bureau of Reclamation's modern dam-safety program.

blocks.title: The Tetons come into the picture
blocks.text: The Teton Range should already be becoming the dominant skyline ahead and slightly to the right. Driggs is still about twenty-six miles away, so this is only the first visual acknowledgment; the main Teton stories will wait until we're much closer.

blocks.title: Crossing toward Teton Valley
blocks.text: We're crossing the broad country west of Teton Valley now. The mountains ahead are doing something unusual visually: instead of gradually rising through foothills, the Tetons seem to leap out of the valley because the range is a fault block with an exceptionally abrupt western and eastern profile.

blocks.title: Young mountains made of ancient rock
blocks.text: The Tetons are geologically young as a mountain range, uplifted for less than about ten million years, yet their highest peaks expose rocks more than two and a half billion years old. That contrast is part of what makes the range so dramatic: young topography cut into extremely ancient crust.

blocks.title: Grand Teton ahead-right
blocks.text: Grand Teton itself should be identifiable ahead-right now as the highest and most commanding summit in the central group. It rises to 13,770 feet. From this western side, the three central Tetons separate particularly well, which is one reason the Idaho view can be so striking.

blocks.title: A range lifted by earthquakes
blocks.text: The range is still rising along the Teton fault. As the region stretches east-west, earthquakes allow the mountain block to tilt upward while the valley side drops. Over many events, that repeated motion created thousands of feet of relief.

blocks.title: Driggs and the west side of the Tetons
blocks.text: Driggs is about seven miles ahead now in the open valley. The town is small enough that the mountain wall still owns the view. Off to the right, the western Teton foothills climb toward Grand Targhee, the ski area that opened in 1969.

blocks.title: Grand Targhee on the west side
blocks.text: Grand Targhee sits in the high country off the right side, west of the main crest. Locals organized the resort in the 1960s, and it opened in December 1969. The resort became one of the defining recreation centers on the Idaho side of the Tetons.

blocks.title: The Driggs Teton view
blocks.text: This is the main west-side Teton viewing window. Keep your attention ahead and to the right. Rather than focusing on one summit, take in the whole wall of peaks rising above the broad agricultural valley; this is the sort of landmark that should be acknowledged before it reaches the wing, not after.

blocks.title: Along the west face
blocks.text: As we turn north at Driggs, the Teton Range stays off the right side. The central peaks are close enough now that individual ridges and snow-holding gullies may stand out, while the valley floor remains broad and comparatively flat.

blocks.title: Glaciers sharpened the peaks
blocks.text: Faulting raised the range, but glaciers did much of the sculpting. Ice widened canyons, sharpened ridges and carved cirques into the high country. The jagged skyline is the combined result of uplift and repeated glaciation.

blocks.title: The range begins to slide behind
blocks.text: The Tetons are still off the right side, but as we continue north they are starting to move from abeam toward right-rear. This is the last good stretch for the central peaks before the route bends northwest toward Ashton.

blocks.title: Tetonia
blocks.text: Tetonia is just ahead in the northern part of Teton Valley. It is a small community, but its position makes it one of the classic west-side gateways to the range; from here the Tetons remain a dramatic eastern backdrop even as our course starts carrying us away from them.

blocks.title: Leaving Teton Valley
blocks.text: We're turning northwest out of the main Teton Valley now. The highest peaks should slip behind-right while the land ahead becomes lower and more rolling. This transition is useful visually because it separates the sharp fault-block mountains from the volcanic country we are about to enter.

blocks.title: The Teton River country
blocks.text: The Teton River drains much of the valley behind us and cuts westward toward the Henrys Fork. The river itself can be hard to follow continuously from altitude, but its green corridor and bends mark the drainage across otherwise open farm country.

blocks.title: Ashton is still ahead
blocks.text: Ashton is still about eight miles ahead, so this is only the regional setup. The town sits near the transition between farm country and the much more heavily forested volcanic plateau leading toward Island Park and Yellowstone.

blocks.title: A small town at a useful crossroads
blocks.text: Ashton grew as a service and transportation center for the surrounding farms and timber country. Its position also made it a natural jumping-off point for the Henrys Fork, Mesa Falls and the roads climbing toward Island Park.

blocks.title: Ashton below
blocks.text: Ashton should be close below now. Ahead, the landscape is about to change quickly: cultivated fields give way to darker forest, river canyons and volcanic terrain tied directly to older phases of the Yellowstone hotspot.

blocks.title: Following the Henrys Fork country
blocks.text: North of Ashton, the Henrys Fork becomes one of the main geographic threads. It drains a remarkable volcanic landscape, cutting through rock produced by older Yellowstone eruptions before eventually joining the Snake River.

blocks.title: Mesa Falls country off the right
blocks.text: The Mesa Falls canyon lies off the right side of this stretch. The waterfalls themselves can be difficult to pick out from nine thousand feet because the river is tucked into forest and canyon walls, so the deeper river cut is the more reliable visual clue.

blocks.title: A waterfall named after an eruption
blocks.text: The name Mesa Falls also belongs to a major volcanic deposit. About 1.3 million years ago, an enormous eruption formed the Henrys Fork caldera and spread the Mesa Falls Tuff across this region. We are flying into the collapsed volcanic center that eruption left behind.

blocks.title: Entering the Henrys Fork caldera
blocks.text: We're now entering the broad Henrys Fork caldera country. Unlike the dramatic bowl people may imagine when they hear the word caldera, much of this one is surprisingly flat because later basalt flows filled its low areas.

blocks.title: Why an old supervolcano can look so ordinary
blocks.text: That flatness is part of the story. After the older rhyolitic magma system cooled, basalt could rise through the crust and spread across the caldera floor. Over time those fluid lava flows buried much of the older relief and produced the smoother landscape below.

blocks.title: Island Park ahead
blocks.text: Island Park is about four to five miles ahead now. Rather than one compact town center, the name applies to a long, spread-out community and recreation area within this forested volcanic basin.

blocks.title: Island Park
blocks.text: This is Island Park country now: lodgepole forest, broad meadows and relatively subdued relief sitting inside an ancient Yellowstone volcanic center. The landscape looks quiet, which makes its explosive geologic history surprisingly easy to underestimate.

blocks.title: From an older Yellowstone to the modern one
blocks.text: Leaving Island Park, we're flying from one of Yellowstone's older volcanic centers toward the modern Yellowstone Plateau. The hotspot did not stay fixed beneath the same piece of crust; North America moved across it, leaving a chain of progressively older volcanic centers southwest across Idaho.

blocks.title: Three great volcanic cycles
blocks.text: The Yellowstone Plateau region records three major caldera-forming cycles in the last roughly two million years: the Huckleberry Ridge event about 2.1 million years ago, the Henrys Fork event about 1.3 million years ago, and the present Yellowstone caldera formed roughly 631 thousand years ago.

blocks.title: Why the plateau looks so forested
blocks.text: The increasingly continuous forest ahead is also tied to geology. Rhyolitic volcanic rocks weather into relatively nutrient-poor, well-drained soils that favor vast lodgepole pine forests, giving much of the Yellowstone Plateau its distinctive dark-green blanket.

blocks.title: West Yellowstone is still ahead
blocks.text: West Yellowstone is still about eight miles ahead. The town became a major western gateway after Union Pacific train service reached it in 1908. Visitors arriving by rail transferred to stagecoaches for the trip into the park, long before private cars became the normal way to tour Yellowstone.

blocks.title: A gateway to a much older human landscape
blocks.text: The railroad story is recent compared with the human history of Yellowstone. Archaeological sites, trails and oral histories show people have used this region for more than eleven thousand years. The modern park boundary came much later, in 1872.

blocks.title: Yellowstone Airport and West Yellowstone
blocks.text: Yellowstone Airport is coming up ahead near West Yellowstone. The airport sits only about two miles from Yellowstone National Park, making this final approach feel like a true gateway rather than just another town stop.

blocks.title: Yellowstone gateway arrival
blocks.text: Yellowstone Airport is about two miles ahead. West Yellowstone and the park entrance lie just beyond. I'll leave you to the arrival from here. When you're finished at Yellowstone Airport, say Trip destination.
